passage:
I am Bidisha, and I am nine. Last Sunday I asked Dadu why we could not eat before the puja, because I was very hungry. Dadu frowned. "Don't answer back. Go and sit down."
I did not answer back. I only asked why. But my face went hot and I ran to my room.
My cousin Kashish came in. "Dadu doesn't mind questions. He minds questions in front of everyone. Write it down, and ask after tea when he's happy."
I wrote it in my notebook and asked after tea. Dadu put down his cup and said, "Come here." He told me a long story about why fasting is done. It was my first time hearing it.

qa.q: How old is Bidisha?
qa.a: Bidisha is nine.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when Dadu said "Don't answer back"?
qa.a: Bidisha felt hurt and confused, since the question was only a "why". The hot face and running to the room show the sting of not being heard.

qa.q: What did Kashish suggest that helped Bidisha get an answer?
qa.a: Kashish suggested writing the question down and asking after tea when Dadu was happy. That gave Bidisha a calm way to be curious without the shame of asking in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Dadu have felt about the question the first time?
qa.a: Dadu may have felt challenged in front of everyone, since Kashish says he minds questions in front of others. Later, over tea, he was glad to explain.

grounding: A child asks an elder a direct question, is told not to answer back, and finds a respectful route to be curious and heard.

passage:
Guest visit note, Tuesday. Nandini, class 4, put up her hand in the assembly when our guest, a retired railway inspector, was speaking. "Sir, why do trains not fall off the bridge when it shakes?" The guest, who prizes discipline, said sternly, "Sit down. Children do not interrupt." Nandini sat, looking at her hands, and her lip trembled.
After assembly I sat beside her. I said, "That was a good question, and there is a time to ask it." We wrote it on a slip and put it in the "Ask the Guest" box. The guest answered it kindly on Friday, with a drawing. Nandini smiled the whole afternoon.
Hansa, class teacher

qa.q: What did Nandini ask the guest?
qa.a: Nandini asked why trains do not fall off the bridge when it shakes.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling as she sat with her lip trembling?
qa.a: Nandini felt embarrassed and hurt. Sitting down and looking at her hands with a trembling lip shows she felt scolded for being curious.

qa.q: What did Hansa do to protect Nandini's curiosity while respecting the guest?
qa.a: Hansa praised the question, wrote it on a slip and put it in the "Ask the Guest" box. That gave Nandini a respectful route to be heard.

qa.q: How might the guest have seen the interruption at first?
qa.a: The guest, who prizes discipline, probably saw it as a break in respect. When the question came by slip, the guest could answer kindly.

grounding: A child asks an elder guest a direct question and is told not to interrupt, and a teacher finds a respectful route for the child to be heard.

passage:
"Jasleen, you ask so many questions. Good. Let me tell you about your Sangeeta Nani when she was nine.
"We lived in Amritsar with my Taya ji, who was very strict. One evening he chased away a stray puppy from our gate with a stick. I asked, 'Taya ji, why can't we keep it? It's so small.' He said, 'Don't answer back to elders,' and walked off. I wasn't answering back. I was asking.
"I cried on the stairs. I thought my questions were bad.
"My Bua found me there. She didn't argue with Taya ji. She gave me an old notebook and said, 'Write your questions here. Every Sunday, bring it to me, and we'll find answers.'
"I filled three notebooks that year. And, Jasleen, the puppy? Bua fed it behind the house. Taya ji pretended not to see.

qa.q: What did Taya ji say when young Sangeeta asked her question?
qa.a: He said, "Don't answer back to elders," and walked off.

qa.q: What was young Sangeeta feeling on the stairs?
qa.a: She felt hurt and confused, crying because she thought her questions were bad when she had only been asking.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Bua gave young Sangeeta a notebook for questions and a Sunday time to discuss them, which kept respect for Taya ji and still gave her curiosity a way to be heard.

qa.q: How might Taya ji have seen the question about the puppy?
qa.a: Taya ji likely saw it as a child challenging his decision, since he valued deference, though later he quietly let the puppy be fed.

grounding: An elder recalls being told not to answer back when she asked a question, and how an aunt gave her curiosity a route to be heard.

passage:
At the crowded family function in Indore, the drums were so loud that Avni had to lean close to shout. All the children were sitting on a mat on the floor while the adults sat on chairs.
Avni tugged Minakshi Mami's sleeve. "Mami, why do children always sit on the floor? The chairs are empty at the back."
Mami frowned. "Don't answer back, Avni. Go sit."
Avni's face burned. She hadn't meant to be rude. She sat down, arms folded, and didn't eat her gulab jamun.
Later, when the music stopped for dinner, her Nani found her in the corner. "What happened, gudiya?"
Avni told her.
Nani nodded. "It was a fair question, asked at a busy time. Mami was rushing. Ask me anything, anytime." Then she walked Avni to the back and they sat on two of the empty chairs together.

qa.q: What were the children sitting on?
qa.a: All the children were sitting on a mat on the floor.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling after Mami told her not to answer back?
qa.a: Avni felt embarrassed and hurt, her face burning, because she hadn't meant to be rude and had only asked a question.

qa.q: How did Nani help Avni, and what could others learn from it?
qa.a: Nani listened, called it a fair question, explained Mami was rushing, and invited Avni to ask anytime, giving her a place to be heard.

qa.q: How might Minakshi Mami have seen the question?
qa.a: Minakshi Mami, busy and rushed at the loud function, likely heard it as a challenge to the elders' rules rather than simple curiosity.

grounding: A child asks an elder a direct question at a busy function and is told not to answer back, and another elder gives her a route to be heard.

passage:
In their Kolkata flat, Bidisha watched Mohit Jethu finish a packet of biscuits on the balcony and toss the wrapper over the railing into the lane.
"Jethu, why do you throw plastic outside? Our teacher says it blocks the drains."
Jethu's face darkened. "Don't answer back to your elders. Your teacher doesn't pay the bills here."
Bidisha went quiet, then went to her room and sat on the bed, hugging her knees.
Her mother came in. "I heard. You weren't rude. You asked a real question."
"Then why did he get angry?"
"Jethu grew up when children didn't ask. It feels strange to him." Ma thought. "Tonight at dinner, let's ask it as a question for everyone: where should our rubbish go?"
At dinner, Bidisha asked. Jethu grumbled, but the next morning a small dustbin appeared on the balcony.

qa.q: What did Jethu throw over the railing?
qa.a: Jethu tossed the biscuit wrapper over the railing into the lane.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha sit hugging her knees?
qa.a: Bidisha felt hurt and confused after being told off for asking a real question she thought was reasonable.

qa.q: What small step did Ma suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Ma suggested asking the question at dinner for the whole family, so Bidisha could be heard without seeming to challenge Jethu alone.

qa.q: How did Jethu likely feel when Bidisha asked her question?
qa.a: Jethu likely felt challenged and a little embarrassed, since he grew up when children did not question elders.

grounding: A child asks an elder a direct question and is told not to answer back, and her mother finds a route for her to be heard.

passage:
"Bade Papa, why did you cut the neem tree? It shaded the whole courtyard."
Darshan lowered his newspaper. "Sachin. Children don't answer back to elders."
"I wasn't answering back. I only asked—"
"Enough."
Sachin's ears went red. He went inside and kicked the doorstop.
Mummy was rolling rotis. "What happened?"
"I asked a question! Now I can't ask anything?"
"You can. Bade Papa grew up where children stayed quiet before elders. On his evening walk, say you've been wondering about the neem, and ask him to tell you."
At dusk Sachin fell into step beside him. "Bade Papa, I keep wondering about the neem. Will you tell me?"
Darshan walked a while. "Its roots were cracking the wall, beta. Your Dada planted it. Cutting it was hard for me too."

qa.q: What was cracking the wall?
qa.a: The neem tree's roots were cracking the wall.

qa.q: How was Sachin feeling when his ears went red?
qa.a: Sachin felt embarrassed and angry, hurt that a real question was treated as rudeness.

qa.q: What helped Sachin get a real answer?
qa.a: Mummy suggested asking on the evening walk, framed as wondering and asking to be told, which gave Sachin a respectful route to be curious.

qa.q: Why might Darshan have snapped "Enough"?
qa.a: Darshan grew up where children stayed quiet before elders, and the neem was painful for him, since cutting a tree Dada planted was hard.

grounding: Shows a child whose direct question is shut down as answering back, and who then finds a respectful way to ask and be heard.
